abstract: Lipid droplets (LDs) store triacylglycerols (TGs) and cholesteryl esters (CEs), but how their relative abundance shapes LD behavior remains poorly understood. CE can form liquid-crystalline (LC) phases and, eventually, crystals. Here, we show that TG acts as a fluidizing component that promotes CE incorporation and controls growth and heterogeneity of CE-containing LDs. Seipin affects TG-rich LDs but has little effect on the size of CE-rich LC LDs. Instead, the TG/CE ratio and lipid deposition history determine whether droplets enlarge, remain isotropic, or enter an LC state. In reconstituted droplets, increasing CE suppresses Ostwald ripening, whereas in cells, the LC state limits incorporation of synthesized neutral lipids. Manipulating DGAT activity shifts LD-phase behavior, consistent with TG synthesis opposing LC organization. Finally, perilipins discriminate between LDs of different compositions: PLIN3 and PLIN5 are depleted from CE-rich LDs, whereas PLIN4 associates better with them. Together, our results establish the TG/CE ratio as a biophysical determinant of LD material state, growth, and protein identity.

summary: TG/CE ratio governs lipid droplet material state, growth, and perilipin identity; TG fluidizes CE, while CE-rich LC droplets resist Ostwald ripening.
title: Triglyceride/cholesteryl ester ratio shapes lipid droplet growth and protein identity.
